questions.q: Why does this lesson say a one-time classification rollout isn't enough on its own?
options: Because labels degrade over time as new data is created and existing data changes, so an ongoing governance program is needed to keep labels accurate
Because classification schemes legally expire after one year
Because a one-time rollout is technically impossible to complete
Because data owners are not allowed to classify more than one dataset per year
questions.explain: Labeling everything once is the easy, visible part; keeping labels accurate as data and people change over time is the harder, ongoing work classification governance exists to do.

questions.q: In the four-role classification governance model, who is responsible for actually implementing the controls (encryption, access restriction, logging) that a classification level requires?
options: The data owner
The data custodian
The governance committee
An external auditor
questions.explain: The data custodian is the technical role that makes a classification's consequences real by implementing the required controls; the data owner decides the classification, and the data steward applies and maintains the label.

questions.q: Which of the following is a real example of 'classification drift' as described in this lesson?
options: A table originally holding only aggregate statistics has a new column added with individual-level data, and nobody revisits its existing Internal label
A data steward correctly re-labels a dataset after a scheduled quarterly review
A governance committee updates the organization's four-tier scheme to five tiers
A data owner initially classifies a new dataset as Confidential
questions.explain: Drift is a dataset's actual sensitivity and its applied label quietly falling out of sync -- exactly what happens when a table's content changes but its label doesn't get revisited.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why are Restricted-tier datasets typically reviewed more frequently than Public-tier datasets in a periodic review cycle?
options: Because Restricted data is reviewed less often, since it rarely changes
Because the cost of an undetected drift is highest for the most sensitive tier, so it earns the most frequent attention within a limited review budget
Because Public-tier data is illegal to review more than once
Review frequency has no relationship to classification tier
questions.explain: Review cycles consume real steward time, so cadence is calibrated by risk -- the highest-risk tiers get the most frequent review since that's where an undetected drift causes the most harm.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the handoff from Chapter 2 (Classification) into Chapter 3 (Access Control)?
options: Chapter 3 replaces the classification scheme entirely with a new one

A classification label only matters if something downstream reads it and acts on it -- Chapter 3's access controls are the first set of controls that take a label as an input and turn it into an actual access decision
Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 cover entirely unrelated topics with no connection
Access Governance must be completed before any data can be classified
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames Chapter 2's labeling work as only mattering once something acts on the label -- Access Governance in Chapter 3 is exactly that first downstream consumer.
